#7472. Most Retail Media Networks Shouldn’t Exist. Here’s How They Can Prove Their Worth

We’re well past the point of oversaturation in ad tech.

There are more than 175,000 software vendors listed on G2, over 15,000 marketing technology solutions and reportedly over 12,000 ad tech vendors in operation. Competitive intensity is real.

But no tech market is more ripe for consolidation than retail media. Look no further than DoorDash’s recent $17 billion acquisition of Instacart. And then there’s Kevel, which supplies ad technology infrastructure to retail media networks and  recently raised $52 million. Its founder and CEO, James Avery, told AdExchanger that a lot of retail media companies are selling to the same customers and that “consolidation is going to happen.”

He also said Kevel likes to joke that “we’re going to help launch 1,000 walled gardens, but then the brands are, like, ‘No, please don’t!’”

The brands are right. For many, the media network model is the wrong bet to make.

Amazon and Walmart took 85.5% of US retail media spend in 2025, leaving only 14.5% for every other network, combined. EMarketer expects this duopoly to take 89% of the growth in 2026 and the share held by every other network it tracks to stay flat or fall through 2027.

Brands haven’t stopped adding networks to their plans, though. McKinsey found that a third of US advertisers used nine or more commerce media networks in 2025. But the reality is that a network can appear on a media plan and still receive very little of the budget.

The same McKinsey survey found that as advertisers add networks, their audiences overlap and the networks become harder to pull apart. Ad buyers told eMarketer much the same thing: They struggle to distinguish one platform from another. The retailer’s brand just isn’t enough of a differentiator.

Too many networks exist without addressing the biggest question: “Why should I be chosen?” Most networks are selling to the same brands and addressing the same audiences, while describing themselves with the same claims about first-party purchasing data and closed-loop measurement. As such, buyers have nothing to base their choice on except for scale and price. And no one beats Amazon there.

The untapped opportunity is for retailers to differentiate their measurement stacks.

In NIQ’s CMO Outlook survey, 67% of CMOs said they planned to increase spending on retail media networks in 2026. Yet only 53% believe today’s networks provide adequate measurement and attribution.

Retailers want to see why each decision in an auction was made: “It’s not enough to say, ‘Trust us, this is doing the best it can for you,’” Kevel’s Avery told AdExchanger.

Advertisers are asking for the same evidence. A brand that can’t compare results across networks will most likely keep its budget where the results are easiest to read.

A retailer’s own shopper data is the one asset no other network can copy. It’s proprietary and unique by definition. But siloing this advantage behind a separate walled login is an expensive and high-friction way of realizing value.

Some retailers have started selling shopper data through partnerships and tools that brands can more easily access.

Tesco, B&Q, John Lewis and Waitrose are piloting dunnhumby’s network alliance, which gives brands a single way to run a campaign across several retailers, with shared standards for measurement and reporting.

Kevel has built API access with Pacvue and Skai along with an integration that lets brands buying Dollar General’s off-site ads through The Trade Desk buy its on-site ads the same way.

In both cases, the retailer still runs its own media business, but brands don’t have to learn its system to buy from it.

Avery expects consolidation among the infrastructure vendors that sell to and support retailers, and Kevel now has the money to win that fight. But advertisers will inevitably consolidate their media plans as well. WARC forecasts that, outside Amazon, global retail media growth will slow to 9.8% in 2027. That’s the lowest rate since it began tracking the market. When growth slows, brands will remove the networks they can’t tell apart or can’t compare on performance.

In 2027, every retail media network will have to answer three questions from the advertisers and agencies it sells to. Why should we choose you over Amazon? Can you prove what our media investment did and compare that to other networks? Can we use familiar tools to buy on your network?

Those who can answer all three questions stand the best chance of being part of the media plan next year.

“Data-Driven Thinking” is written by members of the media community and contains fresh ideas on the digital revolution in media.

#7469. Ad Tech Is Getting Better At Fixing Its Flaws Instead Of Just Calling Them Out, Says DecryptAds’ New COO Arielle Garcia

Constantly pointing out that a system is broken gets old. Eventually, you just want to roll up your sleeves and fix it yourself.

Now, she’s taking on a new role as chief operating officer for advertising cybersecurity startup DecryptAds, the company announced Monday. And Garcia told AdExchanger she believes this will be her most consequential role yet in building a better ad tech industry for advertisers and consumers. In addition to overseeing DecryptAds’ day-to-day operations, she’ll be leading its industry partnerships and engagement with brands, standards bodies and lawmakers.

DecryptAds is building what Edwards describes as his “dream research tool for understanding and tracking publishers and ad systems.”

The company’s goal, Garcia said, is to give researchers, ad agencies, tech companies, industry groups and regulators the evidence they need to identify and fix security gaps in the programmatic supply chain.

DecryptAds examines publicly available data, including ads.txt and sellers.json files, to determine the entities behind publisher sites and ad tech vendors. And it flags when those entities have ties to regions that are sanctioned by the US government or that have high degrees of cybercrime and lax data security practices.

The company is also rolling out a service for notifying clients when other ad systems drop sellers and publishers by examining sellers.json files and tracking API and MCP connections. The service should aid the endless “wack-a-mole” game ad tech vendors have to play to keep their supply chains clean, Garcia said.

She spoke to AdExchanger about promoting industry change through better collaboration in her new role.

ARIELLE GARCIA: The most powerful work that I’ve been a part of is where we take information and bring it to both the market and to government to help inform better decisions or support investigations or lawmaking. For example, when Check My Ads did our Google PMAX research, it wasn’t just a primer on watchouts for small businesses or education for nonprofits. It helped support lawmakers making the case for why regulation wouldn’t break online advertising.

So, when Zach reached out about joining DecryptAds, I was thrilled because what the team is building here is founded on getting information and evidence into everyone’s hands.

You’ve covered how hard it can be for watchdogs to get access to the systems that they’re trying to hold accountable. DecryptAds doesn’t depend on anyone’s permission. It’s built from public data, the files companies are publishing and the infrastructure behind their sites.

In your hiring announcement, you said “After years of identifying the problems in the ad tech ecosystem, I’m proud to be joining a company that’s building a solution.” Does it feel like the industry is getting better at fixing its vulnerabilities rather than just constantly raising the alarm?

The appetite for making this data available is something that’s been growing for a couple of years. We’ve seen this increasingly with the great work Confiant, DeepSee and Adalytics have done.

I’ve had the opportunity to refine my theory of change a bit. There’s an important role for those who are calling out the problems, and there’s an important role for those who are building solutions to fix them. Not everyone is positioned to do both.

But I enjoy working with the industry. And I see changing market behavior as an important lever for improving the industry for marketers, the public and for national security. For me personally, [this role] is an evolution of where I think I can be the most useful.

Will DecryptAds’ research be mainly focused on ad tech cybersecurity or programmatic supply-chain quality? Or are those two inextricably related?

The security framing shows up in how our tool enables the tracing of networks. So understanding that MFA [made-for-advertising] operators and bad actors will try to hide and building that into our capabilities.

But the security ethos also shows up in the spirit of information sharing. That’s why the product has a free researcher tier. Having come from a watchdog organization, I’m excited about giving access to this information to researchers that are currently lacking ways to dig deep into the ecosystem.

It’s been a bad couple of weeks for ad tech cybersecurity news. Are things getting worse, or are they getting easier to catch?

Right, on top of the recent AdFection report by Confiant and Citizen Lab, there’s the military warning that ad data was used to target troops. Also fairly recently, the DOJ bulk data transfer rule. Now you have senators calling for reform in the wake of AdFection.

The government has known for years that ads can be an attack surface. The NSA, CISA and FBI all recommend ad blocking since 2018. But where it used to be more about blocking malicious ads, now there’s more of a realization of the ad system itself being a national security risk.

What’s one way the digital ad industry can work with regulators and researchers to support a safer, more transparent supply chain?

There’s fairly broad recognition of the need for stronger Know Your Customer standards for ad tech. It gets at the core of so many of the scandals that we’ve seen happen over the past few years. And yet trade associations, independent companies and standards bodies aren’t truly embracing the spirit behind that.

How would better Know Your Customer standards work in practice?

DecryptAds has seen how valuable it is to have some type of a geo risk score. It’s fairly easy to determine whether a vendor or a publisher is based in a high-risk or sanctioned jurisdiction. So it’s a strange miss on advertiser verification to not even verify the domain of the advertiser.

And to not have a Know Your Customer vetting process be a part of what TAG [the Trustworthy Accountability Group] expects of certified vendors is surprising to me.

What would you say to companies who might get defensive if they show up in your research?

It’s about collaborating on solutions. It’s always been important to me to be fair and to have receipts. And the goal is never to call out one particular actor when you’re trying to fix a systemic problem. There’s nothing wrong with acknowledging the problem and sharing the steps you’re taking to fix it.

One of the things that was shocking in the wake of the Confiant/Citizen Lab AdFection report was IAB Europe’s reaction, which was to say, the system’s not broken, but it can be exploited.

So accountability in the interest of benefiting everyone should be the goal. And it’s okay to make a mistake or to have an oversight. But it’s not okay to bury our collective heads in the sand as though these are just unfortunate, isolated incidents.

#7467. Why Trade Desk Veteran Jed Dederick Joined The Startup ShopMy To Sell Creator Marketing

Jed Dederick has had an interesting view of the programmatic industry. He was a digital ads seller first at The Wall Street Journal and then WebMD until 2012, when he jumped across the exchange to the still-nascent DSP The Trade Desk.

The rest, as they say, is history. He eventually led all TTD sales as CRO, and had industry stage time as an expert witness throughout the Department of Justice’s publisher ad tech antitrust suit against Google.

But this month is Dederick’s first as CRO of ShopMy, a marketplace that connects marketers to social and online creators.

“In a world where the older forms of performance marketing like search are seeing massive declines and are in huge question,” creator content is ready to step up, he told AdExchanger.

We caught up with Dederick about the new role and how, practically speaking, social creator commerce can become an always-on paid performance channel.

DEDERICK: I have lots of experience with how ads have funded the distribution of content and information. The thing that stood out to me was how crowded and commoditized paid advertising has become.

[ShopMy] has this idea that there’s all of this value and performance locked up inside creator content. Brands see it with high conversion rates and success rates with individual creator relationships, but haven’t had real scale or measurability.

And I see a tremendous amount of untapped performance marketing value in the creator commerce world. I mean, for instance, if you’re interested in buying the best mosquito zapper, that’s easier now than it’s ever been.

The process of discovery, inspiration and purchase is happening inside the creator landscape. And there are huge pockets of individual value that haven’t been tied together.

Creators sign up for free, though we have to approve them. And they’re earning a commission on sales.

On the brand side, it’s a subscription model.

Anybody who’s worked on the brand side in creator influencer marketing knows it’s really painful to set up an individual relationship with a creator. The trade-off for that one relationship hasn’t always translated into a massive vehicle or a line item for performance marketing. And so what we’re doing is making it possible for a brand to reach thousands of valuable creators at once through one central place.

Does ShopMy have its own app or is it only plugged into affiliate networks and places where products are sold?

Our creators are putting up content in a lot of places [with affiliate marketing programs]. Meta is certainly one. Substack is one. TikTok is one. And understanding that creators have a lot of platforms to put out content, ShopMy is a central place for brands and creators.

Traditionally, brands have had to go to multiple places to manage individual creator relationships or rely on platform reporting from all the different places those creators can be. [ShopMy] is an easy way to gain promotion by creators without having to create individual, unique sponsorships with the creators.

And, I’ll also add, we’ve launched a shopper app very recently.

We’re doing $1.9 billion in GMV [“gross merchandise volume,” for the uninitiated] right now. So I think part of why this probably isn’t in the lexicon is that [ShopMy] has lived a lot in the commerce landscape, particularly in fashion and beauty.

But you can see why I look at this from a performance marketing lens and think, “Oh my goodness! If only the brands that I know and have worked with could run this way and think this way. This doesn’t need to just live in one pocket of the ecosystem.”

Who are you dealing with at an advertiser client? The “affiliate person” in the marketing org could be very different from the “performance marketing person.”

This is why I’m here. This is what I think is fun: busting up the old silos in the name of value and efficiency.

I mentioned that we have thousands of premium brand partners, like Jimmy Choo, for the sake of example. Those types of brands have had creator teams and affiliate teams, right? Sometimes they sit under PR. Sometimes it’s under the umbrella of social or paid media.

Brands have organized themselves that way because that’s been the opportunity so far. But what I do is I bring scale and liquidity that can make [creator content] basically a vehicle for what would have been performance marketing and paid media budgets.

In terms of working with hundreds of thousands of creators – orthodontists, baristas, airline stewardesses and endlessly on – how are they selling general stuff?

I think this idea is so much bigger than it currently is.

People’s social circles are how we’ve gotten trusted recommendations forever. Your friends or someone you trust in a field have given you recommendations, and those are way more powerful than anything you’ve gotten through paid ads.

There are people in our network across lots of disciplines who have their own followings in their fields. So, sure, in that case, that might be relevant for endemic brands. But an orthodontist might be relevant for oral care and personal care brands. Creators post lifestyle-oriented [content] across categories: be it travel, fashion, cosmetics.

The reality of this landscape is how we get recommendations that used to be from our friends, maybe a co-worker, someone from a group chat. That’s the basis for what we’re scaling with creators.

Is there a brand safety/verification-type partner?

The reality is that how we think of user-generated and quote-unquote “premium” content is less helpful now. I don’t know about you, but when I go home, I turn on Netflix, and I see YouTube creators on Netflix. What my family’s watching is YouTube creators on Netflix with longer-format shows.

The world has changed quite a bit. There’s authentic content that connects, and there’s everything else.

#7464. Going Straight To The C-Suite; All I Want For Christmas Is Hess Truck Ads In September

Pinch your nose and blow gently through your nostrils.

That’s how to unpop your eardrums on a plane, or after taking the elevator from the lowly marketer offices to the executive floor.

Earlier this month, this newsletter noted the trend of holdco CEOs making handshake deals with brand CEOs to poach accounts their agencies didn’t even pitch. That’s the theory behind Publicis landing PepsiCo, Microsoft and LVMH.

Deloitte Digital is another example, as Digiday reports. The marketing consultancy arm of Deloitte’s holdco is going straight to CEOs to pitch its new enterprise operating system.

Traditionally, the marketing department has been Deloitte’s target and entry point. But the kind of enterprise deal it’s now seeking requires CEO approval and is part of a “more executive conversation,” says Deloitte Digital US CMO Mark Singer.

Plus, Deloitte’s product is called Converge Front Office (or “CFO,” lol).

The product name is fitting, as Gartner VP Jay Wilson perhaps unwittingly notes, since CFOs are taking bigger roles in evaluating marketing spend: “Increasingly, we see and hear from clients and agencies that the CFO is the critical piece of the new business puzzle, as marketing budgets remain flat.”

Deloitte Digital’s thinking is that brands have archives of back-filled content, copy and campaigns that haven’t been touched in ages. So why not have AI agents upcycle that content instead of buying more?

Gotta hand it to them; it’s definitely not a holdco pitch.

It’s not just you – the Christmas creep started creeping even earlier this year.

This September, there were 11% more holiday-themed ads on TV than in 2025 and six times more than in 2021, according to Nielsen.

Not surprisingly, retailers are on track to spend the most of any ad vertical. They made up almost 64% of all holiday ads aired on linear TV in October, which actually outpaces their usual holiday ad blitz. Over the past five years, retail accounted for about 45% of holiday ads across both linear and streaming TV.

Nielsen also notes some historical trends that could factor into this holiday season. For instance, there were a lot more automotive holiday ads on streaming (18.4%) than there were on linear (9.7%) last year. Maybe it’s a way to appeal to cord-cutting millennials who’ve started saying “Happy Honda Days” to each other as a bit.

But does running holiday ads sooner get consumers to spend more throughout the season?

According to Deloitte’s annual holiday shopping survey (which was conducted between late August and early September), the average household spend will increase 4% to $1,654 this year. And, while 22% of consumers plan to shop earlier this year, they expect 28% of their budgets to be spent by the end of October – the highest share Deloitte has seen in six years.

So total holiday spending may be up a bit. But it won’t pay to wait until Mariah Carey is fully thawed to run those ads.

The global internet is getting less global. And questions that once seemed outright crazy – such as, “Might Meta stop doing business in the European Union?” – are not so crazy anymore.

There’s no urgent crisis for Meta. The canary in the coal mine is really X. Elon Musk has threatened to stop serving X users in Europe going back to 2023 and fumed over a $140 million Digital Services Act fine last year.

But as Eric Seufert notes at Mobile Dev Memo, there’s a confluence of problems in Europe for Meta that could force its hand.

The EU’s anti-personalization rules and requirement that Meta offer an ad-free subscription service have also decreased the platform’s advertising payouts.

Plus, the European Commission’s Digital Fairness Act is taking shape. It would prohibit common mobile game monetization tactics like offering virtual in-game currencies or letting users pay for “variable-reward systems” (aka loot boxes). If mobile games make less money in the EU, that means smaller budgets for mobile app advertising, which is a revenue pillar for Meta.

At some point, these things add up. And, eventually, staying in the EU may not make mathematical sense for Meta.

#7462. Websites Aren’t Just For People Anymore. Here’s How Marketers Optimize Them For Agents

It’s always nice for a marketer to get a compliment on their website. But does the compliment still resonate when it comes from an AI agent?

Ask again in a few months and we might have an answer.

On Tuesday, customer journey intelligence platform Knotch announced a new solution called Ace for Agents. The product builds on its existing AI marketing solution, Ace, but is specifically focused on making website content more accessible to AI agents.

But what does it mean for content to be accessible to agents that, by definition, can access pretty much all content across the web?

Effectively, it involves reformatting content into simpler terms and unifying it from multiple sources onto a single webpage, said Andrew Bolton, chief customer officer at Knotch.

Most LLM crawlers declare themselves when they access a webpage, so Knotch knows to show them the AI version of a page, said Bolton. For those that don’t declare, Ace can analyze actions like on-site behavior to determine that the viewer is a bot.

AI agents, unlike humans, don’t care about interactive features or aesthetically pleasing graphics. Instead, their focus is on brevity and direct statements.

Often, the reformatting includes adding FAQs and concise summaries, as well as removing JavaScript. The result is a pared-down version of the webpage a human would see, but the key content remains.

That’s what Bolton describes as a one-to-one version of an existing webpage, in which the information that’s already on it is simply restructured, but nothing new is added. That’s one of the two types of pages that Ace for Agents can develop – the simpler, “v1” offering, said Bolton.

The slightly more advanced version of Ace for Agents involves “injecting new components of information” from other sources of the brand’s choosing, he said, like third-party review sites, or the brand’s own YouTube channel.

For instance, he added, if a car manufacturer had a particularly favorable review on a third-party site comparing one of its models to a competitor’s model, Knotch can ingest that into the manufacturer’s context model.

Reviews “would be valuable to a consumer who’s trying to evaluate those two different vehicles,” he added. Marketers have a say on whether they want to manually flag external reviews and other content to pull in, or if they want to use an agent to automatically pull in new, positive content, which a human can then review.

The resulting webpage is a “super piece of content” that is able to “combine the atoms” of several different pages across the web, said Bolton. Now, an LLM only needs to access one page, but gets the same amount of data that it historically would’ve collected from crawling all of the data sources individually.

It’s worth noting that the data inputs are entirely curated by the brand. In other words, the good reviews will be ingested, and the bad ones won’t. A brand wouldn’t elect to put negative reviews on their website, Bolton said, and Knotch is effectively creating an agent-readable webpage that pulls all of the informative and positive information on the brand into a single source.

As marketing and the open web rapidly evolve, agencies need to build an “experience that reaches both the people and the machines,” Melissa Berger, chief solutions officer at Digitas, told AdExchanger. “Earning attention” has always been a major focus for the agency, Berger said, “and now that’s not just earning from the human; it’s earning from the agents, too.”

Digitas has been working with Knotch for over a year and began testing Ace for Agents several months ago as a way to earn some of that agentic attention.

Although Ace for Agents has been a good way for brands to increase discoverability, they still need to understand who their human customers are, said Berger. Otherwise, the LLM-accessible site may be full of information, but not have the answers to the specific questions the humans are looking for.

Once a brand understands exactly what sort of questions its customers are asking and what queries it should aim to show up against, said Berger, “the rest of the content is updated to be catered more toward that.”

#7458. Ad Tech Doesn’t Need Another Tool. It Needs Fewer Handoffs

Every few months, we get excited about an industry update, like a new ad format or AI tool. That energy is a big part of what keeps ad tech moving forward, but I believe the next five years will be shaped less by any single innovation and more by how well the tools we already have work together.

The marketing technology landscape has 15,384 solutions and counting. The opportunity now is in the gaps between them, because that’s where time, data and trust get lost.

Think about a typical day for an affiliate. They usually juggle several platforms to find offers and buy traffic. And when it comes to site or landing-page monetization, that can mean yet another platform. On top of that, they have to keep track of balances and compare reports.

Together, these tools power decisions about budgets and traffic. But every handoff takes time, and some data inevitably gets lost along the way.

Agencies feel it, too. At POSSIBLE earlier this year, the conversation turned to whether AI can finally break down those silos and perhaps eliminate a few steps along the way.

The most important handoff in any AI workflow is the one from data to decision. AI can generate advertising copy and visuals very quickly at scale. But it can also optimize areas outside of the creative process: identifying outliers, explaining why a campaign behaves as it does, suggesting improvements, matching traffic with the right offers and taking over repetitive tasks.

What we don’t discuss enough, however, is that AI is only as good as the data it works with. If the data is flawed or weak, all AI can do is help you make the wrong decision faster. Before automating decisions, it’s worth making sure you can trust the data.

Some of the riskiest handoffs are the ones we don’t control at all, especially our dependence on platforms that can change the rules overnight.

Changes like these will keep coming. However, there is something we can do: Build businesses that adapt quickly. When the parked-domain change happened, RollerAds didn’t start from scratch; we adapted the traffic monetization infrastructure we already had to work with domain traffic. In my experience, that’s what most real innovation looks like: spotting a shift early and building on what you already do well.

The last handoff is between partners, and it only works if both sides trust what they’re seeing.

Advertisers need to trust their partner platform and the traffic this platform provides. Publishers need to be able to predict their earnings. Affiliates need their conversions reported accurately. A great interface makes all of this easier to see, but what earns trust is what’s underneath: reliable tracking, fraud protection and clear, honest communication.

If I could ask the industry for one thing, it would be to make ad tech understandable.

At its core, the idea of digital advertising is simple: Show people relevant ads. But, over time, it has grown into a complex mix of acronyms, integrations and dashboards.

Here’s my invitation to every platform: Before shipping the next feature, count the handoffs it removes. That’s the thinking behind RollerAds as a full-cycle ad platform. We’ve brought buying traffic, monetizing sites and running offers together in one account, and we keep looking for more steps to remove. The next big thing in ad tech may not be a thing at all. It will be the stage when tools combine into one seamless process with fewer handoffs, data we can trust, businesses that can absorb change and partners who make hard things simpler.

#7453. Mark Vins’ ‘Reef to Ridge’ premiered at TIFF. Now pocket.watch is on board as its distributor.

After building brands alongside some of YouTube’s biggest kid-friendly stars, pocket.watch is increasing its presence in the world of film distribution. The creator media company has come on board as the exclusive worldwide distributor and sales agent for Reef to Ridge, a nature documentary directed by Brave Wilderness Co-Founder and CEO Mark Vins.

Reef to Ridge takes viewers to the Galapagos Islands, where Vins and his crew explore unique habitats, encounter endangered species, and discuss the challenges that hinder conservation efforts around the world. The project premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) where it was part of a showcase curated by YouTube. By highlighting projects from creators like Vins and Ziwe, YouTube showed that its biggest draws were ready for Hollywood close-ups.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

By working with Vins to give Reef to Ridge a streaming premiere, pocket.watch is solving a problem that has stunted progress for some creators with Hollywood ambitions. Major studios are eager to turn YouTube stars into feature directors, but the distributors attached to those projects have often been film industry firms like A24 and Neon. Meanwhile, creators who eschew traditional distribution can encounter some headaches, as Markiplier discovered when he attempted to bring his video game adaptation Iron Lung to YouTube.

As a creator media company, pocket.watch can pursue global distribution for a project like Reef to Ridge while also understanding the needs of a director like Vins. “Creators have built extraordinary relationships with their audiences, and there is a real opportunity to bring that connection to feature films,” said pocket.watch Founder and CEO Chris M. Williams in a statement. “Mark Vins and his team have made a visually striking, cinematic film with the ambition and scale to reach well beyond their established fanbase. We’re bringing our distribution expertise and platform partnerships to that opportunity, with more creator-led film announcements to come.”

As Williams alluded to in his statement, Reef to Ridge is just the start for pocket.watch. The media company is going to help creators realize their feature film ambitions. According to a press release, more announcements of this nature will arrive “by year’s end.”

#7451. Which social platforms do Americans use to communicate? Depends who you ask.

The Pew Research Center has delivered its annual report on U.S. social media usage, and as per usual, there are some revealing trends lurking within the demographic data. YouTube is still the most ubiquitous social platform among Americans, but beyond the top spot, the rankings differ depending on factors like age, gender, household income, and political orientation.

In last year’s Pew report, the top-ranked finishers were the platforms that best reached older Americans, and in 2026, that trend has essentially held true. YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram went 1-2-3 in the overall ranking and were the most-used social hubs in the 65-and-older age bracket.

The platforms on the rise include some apps focused on communication. Adoption of both Snapchat and WhatsApp rose 1% year-over-year, but those companies are making gains within different communities. Snapchat’s user base still skews toward female users — it reaches 30% of U.S. women and 21% of U.S. men — while WhatsApp now reaches a higher percentage of U.S. men, which wasn’t the case a year ago.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Stats related to household income are also noteworthy. Snapchat is more common in U.S. households that make less than $70,000 per year, while WhatsApp reaches its highest percentage of Americans (40%) in households that eaern at least $100,000 per year.

In general, social media use seems to be stratifying. Platforms like Facebook and TikTok tend to be more common in lower-income households. LinkedIn, as you would expect, appeals to Americans who are more well-off.

The economic polarization of U.S. social media can best be seen by examining the adoption of Nextdoor, which is a relatively new addition to Pew’s annual reports. The proportion of Americans using Nextdoor has risen by 5% over the past five years, but the community-oriented app is growing in particular communities. Only 9% of Americans in households making $30,000 or less per year use Nextdoor; in households where annual income exceeds $100,000, that percentage jumps to 23%.

Are there any clear takeaways from these economic conditions? Perhaps some marketers will want to adjust platform spend to meet target consumers where they spend the most time. But the Pew rankings also show us that U.S. social media is inherently mutable. Beyond YouTube’s hold on the top spot, there’s plenty of room for change in each year’s rankings.

#7445. Top 5 Branded Videos of the Week: Golf is happening

Welcome to our rundown of the most-watched branded YouTube videos of the week.

We’re publishing this snippet of a larger Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report in order to analyze sponsorship trends in the creator economy. Any video launched in tandem with an official brand partner is eligible for t he ranking.

And–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats. If you’re interested in learning more about Gospel–and which brands are sponsoring what creators on YouTube–click here. You can also download our YouTube 2025 Sponsorship Landscape Report here.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Boxing, golf, and football reign supreme in this week’s Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report, with sponsorships from DAZN, DraftKings, Lowe’s, and more.

#1 The Boy Who Punched Back ?? Channel: Zack D. Films Brand: DAZN Views: 13,632,976

Zack D. Films‘ DAZN promo starts like a Dhar Mann video: A kid, relentlessly bullied, finally has enough and stands up to his schoolyard oppressors.

The Short keeps this inspirational tone, but it swings toward sports. Viewers learn the “kid” is actually world champion boxer Canelo Álvarez, and that after spending years at the top of his sport, he was defeated. Now, at 36, he wants to reclaim one of his old titles–World Boxing Council super middleweight champion–and to clinch it, he has to go up against undefeated young gun Christian Mbilli.

And, of course, that match can only be watched on DAZN. The sports-specific streamer has been in our space since the Logan Paul vs KSI days, and continues to partner with creators for special events.

#2 64 Golfers Compete For 4 Million Dollars | Internet Invitational Episode 1 Channel: Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, Barstool Sports, Internet Invitational Brand: Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, ZYRTEC Views: 12,095,382

And video #1 isn’t the only sports championship in the cards this week.

Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, and Barstool Sports brought 64 creator golfers together for the Internet Invitational, which will pit them against each other on the green until just one puts their way to victory.

Episode 1 of this tournament is over five hours long–which is a lot of airtime for sponsors Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, and ZYRTEC. We’re obviously intrigued by the tourney’s player lineup (which includes Dude Perfect‘s Tyler Toney, former Good Good-er Grant Horvat, TikToker Josh Richards, and Nelk Boys member Salim, with Barstool’s Dave Portnoy and pro golfer Kevin Kisner as rules officials), but we’re also intrigued by the brand choices. There’s some hefty companies here.

DraftKings is basically a ubiquitous presence these days no matter which sport you’re watching–or which YouTube video. It paid for more than 80 videos this week alone. Then there’s Zyrtec, which we supposes connects here because these golfers are getting snootfuls of grass out on the green. (This is the only video Zyrtec sponsored.) Dunkin and Reese’s round out the snacks-and-drinks set, and prove once again that major food n bev brands are firmly committed to spending their marketing budgets in our space.

#3 Making the worlds most extreme candy (it short-circuits my brain) Channel: NileBlue Brand: Brilliant Views: 12,475,822

He’s one of our few non-sports entrants this week, but NileBlue is still getting into the ring–and putting his tongue on the line.

His thesis is simple: candies like Warheads are trying to give the eater a truly unpleasant experience. But none of them are quite overwhelming enough.

“I think this is mostly because they’re all trying to only assault one thing at a time,” Nile says. “Which personallly, I think is a mistake, because it leaves so many completely available tastebuds completely unaffected. And what I really want is a candy that targets everything.”

That means a candy which is sour, sweet, spicy, icy, bitter, salty, and umami to the max, all at the same time.

Can he succeed? Viewers who lock in for his full 38-minute journey will be rewarded with the answer (and sponsor Brilliant will be rewarded with their watch time).

#4 LIVE with Lowes playing Madden 27, featuring Justin Jefferson! #ad Channel: MMG Brand: Lowe’s Views: 11,333,221

Our final sports video of the week is from OG Madden YouTuber MMG, who’s joined by Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson for a chat and a few rounds in Madden 27.

The YouTube world and the sports world are becoming increasingly intertwined (just look at the above creator invitational, for example), so it’s not as unusual to see athletes popping up on creators’ channels, but it’s still cool every time. MMG launched his channel in 2015, and after 11 years of work, he’s sitting pretty with NFL stars.

This stream was part of the Lowe’s “Earn Your Sunday” campaign, which urges dudes to get their sh*t done around the house so they can kick back and watch the weekend games. As part of the deal, MMG gave away a signed Jefferson helmet and jersey; viewers who head over to the Lowe’s website will also see another, bigger giveaway for the “ultimate Super Bowl Sunday.” Lowe’s is definitely putting stock into making the end of this NFL season a touchdown.

BONUS #2,410 I Played Skyrim as a Lore Accurate Vampire Channel: OSK Gaming Brand: Idle Obelisk Miner Views: 124,561

In honor of everyone who waited 15 years for a name reveal, we brought in OSK Gaming and his very dedicated Skyrim playthrough as our bonus video.

Bethesda Game Studios boss Todd Howard has a contentious reputation among gamers, and OSK has another gripe for the pile: He’s pretty sure the ol’ Todd hates vampires. So what’s a guy to do if he wants to play a real vampire within the sprawling fantasy world of Skyrim? You download a boatload of mods and do it yourself. Who cares if Skyrim won’t let you be a real vampire? OSK is gonna make it happen anyway.

On his journey, he’ll actually be playing two games, thanks to his sponsor Idle Obelisk Miner. As you may expect from the name, IOM is an idle title, where you get set up and then all you have to do is check in on things every once in a while. What you might not expect is that one game title would sponsor a video about another completely unrelated game. But this is the perfect pairing. While OSK hikes across Skyrim, IOM runs in the background, so he can game while he games.

…and there’s a lot more data where that came from. If you like our Weekly Top 5, you’ll love everything else Gospel has to offer.

#7442. The IAB has had enough: It’s calling on platforms to standardize the definition of a “view”

When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it said its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.

The new counts, it said, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”

But the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation. Data from Agentio showed public viewcounts over-reported actual views by 40%; experiments by individual creators like John Green, who compared his backend viewcount of one video to its public-facing count, found similar inaccuracy.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, the Interactive Advertising Bureau has released a report, The Creator Economy’s Next Chapter, that calls for wide standardization of what counts as a “view.”

Accurate measurement is the “fault line beneath the creator economy,” the IAB said in its report. This overall conclusion came from 53 participating industry leaders who filled out the IAB’s survey, and also from senior industry leader interviews conducted by the IAB’s Creator Economy Board.

“Measurement also sits inside problems that look like something else. Two sides who disagree on creator pricing both agree they cannot judge whether creators are paid fairly because nobody agrees what creator content is worth,” the IAB wrote. “One in eight respondents traced budget fights with leadership to measurement gaps, and a similar share said organizations withhold results because the numbers behind them are not solid enough to publish.”

We see why this is a major concern: Brands pay creators based on their reach, so when platforms like YouTube roll out changes that inflate views, marketers end up overpaying.

It might not sound bad for creators to make a little extra cash, but this situation doesn’t end well for them either. If they secure a brand deal based on inflated views, that sets a high bar for engagement that their sponsored content almost certainly will not clear. This performance gap might result in them losing their relationship with that individual brand, or with an entire agency that represents other important brands in their niche.

It’s not just marketers that told the IAB standardization is needed. “Measurement providers, who see the problem most closely, were unanimous in choosing a common definition of a view as a top priority,” the bureau said in its report.

They also have a proposed solution: “Respondents are clear about where to start. Given 11 possible standards, two-thirds (66%) chose a common definition of a view and exposure metrics across platforms,” per the report. “Each platform counts a view differently, and shared reporting format, cross-channel planning, and any comparison with video or television all depend on counting it the same way.”

Among the IAB’s respondents, another interesting data point emerged. The majority of entities that produce metrics (like platforms, marketing agencies, and measurement companies) say they are “very confident” in the accuracy of the numbers they provide.

Meanwhile brands and talent agencies both said they have zero percent confidence in numbers they receive.

The IAB says to rectify this problem, it plans to work alongside the Media Ratings Council and other “engaged industry bodies” to bring content platforms and measurement providers together so everyone can agree on cross-platform definitions of a view, an impression, reach, and watch time.

It says it hopes to secure one to two platform agreements within the first year of this effort.

If it does that, we might be looking at one of the biggest industry shifts to date, and could end up in a radically different era of social media and content creation.

35% of respondents said creators’ work split across teams and tools is not working. 33% said brands don’t understand creators’ channels. 31% cited pricing inconsistency, and 25% said agreeing on contract and deal terms is difficult.

Solutions they suggested include standard T&Cs and contracts for creator x bran deals (66% of respondents), transparency standards for agency fee disclosure (38%), and a unified creator taxonomy (31%).

#7438. Top Million Sites Lost 12% Of Visits; Top 100’s Share Barely Moved via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Learn how to prioritize page fixes, check agent access and measure readiness for your 2027 SEO plan.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Data shows visits to the world's top million websites declined from an earlier peak, visits going to sites outside the top 100 barely changed.

Visits to the world’s top million websites were lower in the third quarter of 2026 than at their early 2022 peak (a decline of 12.2%), based on the data from Similarweb shared by SparkToro. The proportion of visits that go to websites that are not among the top 100 stayed relatively consistent over this time. That means while the total number of visits was down, that proportion still added up to less traffic for non-top-100 sites.

Rand Fishkin, SparkToro’s co-founder and CEO, wrote that the project began with his theory that the biggest sites, largely Big Tech properties, were taking more of the web’s traffic.

The post also reports a 29.2% drop in visits per internet user. This calculation uses user estimates that were revised partway through the period.

Fishkin asked Similarweb for total visits to the top million sites from its worldwide desktop and mobile web panel, along with a breakdown by site rank.

In the post’s figures, total visits peaked in Q1 2022 at 2.243 trillion. At the low point in Q1 2026, the total was 1.914 trillion, down 14.7% from the peak. The latest quarter, Q3 2026, came in at 1.970 trillion, 12.2% below the peak.

The totals on the post’s chart stay roughly level through 2023, then dip in early 2024 and fall again in the first half of 2025.

Similarweb categorized the top million websites from the number 1-10 to the 100,001st to 1 millionth website by five levels of ranking.

The share chart shows roughly a combined 33% and 36% of visits for the #1-10 (top) and #11-100 (next 90) sites during Q4 2021 and Q3 2026 respectively. The percentages for each band below the top 100 were a little lower at the end of the period compared to the beginning.

Fishkin described growth in the share for the top 100 as small, writing that “stagnation is a more accurate description of the trend.”

SparkToro’s per-user number is found by dividing Similarweb’s total visits by DataReportal’s estimated quarterly internet users globally. The table included in the blog post reports 4.95 billion internet users in Q4 2021 and 6.15 billion for Q3 2026. This represents an increase of around 24% during that time. The blog post reports the decline in visits per user at 29.2%.

The user series jumped from 5.65 billion to 6.04 billion in one quarter (Q3) of 2025. According to DataReportal in their October 2025 report, this jump in the number of users online was “largely attributable to significant revisions” in the rate of internet use that were officially reported by India and China. They also warned the reader to avoid interpreting this change as if hundreds of millions of new people came online in 90 days.

The SparkToro post did not include information regarding the change in reporting. Their estimate of 24% user growth compared data prior to and subsequent to the reporting change.

Similarweb’s panel tracks browser visits on desktop and mobile, but not app use. Fishkin wrote that consolidation by Big Tech is likely much more common in apps.

The data is also worldwide, and he wrote that it’s plausible traffic to U.S., U.K. and EU sites declined while regions with growing internet access, such as Asia and Africa, grew. The post doesn’t break out regions or state the panel’s size.

He did not provide reasons for the decline in visits. Fishkin’s list of possible factors includes app-only use, reliance on search engine results, AI tool utilization, social media platforms and the user behavior changes after the COVID-19 pandemic.

After initial publication SparkToro updated their article. On Nov. 10, Fishkin said on X that the prior version of his post “had an incorrect graph/data.” That version’s headline put the decline at 24%, which the URL still shows.

SparkToro sells audience research software, and Fishkin co-authored the book “Zero Click Marketing.”

SparkToro has provided an international benchmark for when a multi-year traffic decline shows up in your reports. The percentage of visits based upon the ranking of the website held close to steady in Similarweb’s browser-based metrics, although the actual number of visits decreased. The headline statistic in the report without reliance on changes in user estimates is the 12.2 percent decline in overall visits.

This report measures the number of browser visits to the top million websites regardless of where they came from, whereas the zero-click data I reported on back in June measured clicks per U.S. Google search.

Until a regional breakdown is available, SparkToro’s figures are best viewed as global context for traffic conversations, rather than as a benchmark for any single market. Fishkin also wrote that he plans to compare the findings with other sources and revisit the numbers every year or two.

#7435. New report claims TikTok Live is fastest-growing platform for game streaming

As TwitchCon descends upon San Diego, a different hub for video game streaming is celebrating its ascendance. TikTok Live is the fastest growing platform in that category, according to a new report published by the GameSquare subsidiary Hatchet.

Hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.

Previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals. While TikTok Live watch time grew 96% year-over-year, Twitch and YouTube Gaming’s respective market shares both went down.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Through properties like Hatchet, FaZe Clan, and TubeBuddy, GameSquare has made deep inroads in digital gaming communities. “Hatchet’s latest report shows just how quickly TikTok Live has established itself in gaming live-streaming,” said GameSquare CEO Justin Kenna in a statement. “Nearly doubling its gaming hours watched in a year is a clear signal that audience habits are shifting toward mobile, discovery-driven viewing.”

Kenna cited titles like Roblox, Garena Free Fire, and Mobile Legends as three major drivers of TikTok Live’s watch time uptick. Roblox led all games in terms of TikTok Live watch time during the first half of 2026; it generated 631 million hours of TikTok viewership during that period.

Roblox is a favorite of Gen Alpha gamers, while Free Fire and Mobile Legends appeal to gamers on mobile devices, especially outside of the United States. Those two data points help explain how TikTok Live has managed such a sizable gaming glow-up — it has volume none of its competitors can match. With 1.4 million creators active each day, TikTok Live’s community is nearly twice as big as Twitch’s.

That massive quantity has made TikTok Live a market leader across multiple streaming categories. Its gaming operation, however, is one of its strongest fortes, and rival platforms should be prepared to see more growth from their ByteDance-owned competitor.

Affiliate links still help protect your commissions as AI checkout grows, while stronger tracking and better program choices help preserve referral credit.

This week’s Ask an SEO is about affiliate marketing, which is actually one of my favorite topics to cover.

“With Google’s UCP and checkout happening inside Gemini and AI Mode, the shopper never clicks my link. Does the affiliate model survive this, and what should I be doing now?”

Great question, and yes, affiliate links still matter, so make sure you keep using them. It is similar to Shopify having the Google Direct Checkout UCP. That doesn’t mean you don’t need to keep your Shopify store, but you also want to make sure you are protected with multiple ways to monetize and that you work with brands that focus on more than just links.

This is why there is a question. If the person doesn’t make it to the link, do links matter? Yes, and this goes back to the history of links.

I was on a call once where we decided that if there was an affiliate parameter and if it was on the browser, the website would automatically prompt the person to log in. This was high-tech back then.

The message displayed was a benefit to them, to let them know that if they logged in, they could add to their cart and check out later when they have more time vs. needing to do everything right now. When they logged in, we could sync up the sale with the original click, and the affiliate would get credit. This led to fingerprinting and many more advanced techniques the networks (like Buy.at at the time) began working on.

There are also affiliate companies that show ads via streaming TV shows and track the IPs connected to the same connection to track affiliate sales back. They count the IPs against consumer data sent back to the network and get credit for the sale.

The reason I mention this is because, clicks don’t always matter, but they do add levels of tracking security for you. There is IP hashing, companies like TV Scientific and AudioHook are using alternative tracking methods, and vanity codes. Just make sure your vanity code doesn’t get leaked to coupon websites, browser extensions, and that AI doesn’t start showing them to traffic you didn’t refer.

See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It

Being afraid of Google taking the order and cutting your link out is a valid concern. But think about TikTok Shop, or retailer apps inside ChatGPT like Walmart’s, which keep the purchase on the platform. These cut your link out completely. The person may read your content then go to TikTok for a review and purchase there.

You have big brands that allow third parties to sell on their website (i.e., marketplaces), and with some you don’t get commissions for those sales as they’re third party vendors. Your links matter and clicks tracked, but the conversion is not commissionable. In the case of systems like TikTok, use links on your website and upload content to their platform to make money with your vendors that are synced there. You control the situation, don’t stress over a single link on the website.

For programs that allow third-party sales and don’t pay, select other programs. That is a choice you are knowingly making and you are knowingly sending your traffic there.

See also: Getting Your Product Into ChatGPT Isn’t The Hard Part, Getting It Through Checkout Is

Another reason to not stop using affiliate links is that consumers do not trust AI. Keynote speakers at college graduations keep getting booed when they talk about it; younger generations are avoiding brands that use it for creating images; people are starting to engage less with AI ads on social media and convert less when the content and images are clearly AI on a website (blog posts, product pages, etc.).

When AI is used, there’s no way to know if the store and ad are legit, or if they’re a third-party counterfeit produced overseas. Reviews are also being gamed. Consumers may not trust the AI Overview as much if quality doesn’t improve, and if they don’t like AI, they will instead scroll down to your content, where they can be exposed to your link.

There is another layer to affiliate links mattering as well.

AI Overviews cannot demonstrate a product or service. Yes, they can play a video, but Google search has done this for years. People, especially those who do not trust AI, will keep looking for human-created content before making the purchase. This is especially true for larger-ticket items like bikes, software, or computer systems, and demonstrations of video games before buying them. Think of parents who want to make sure it is age-appropriate, or someone who wants to see what the graphics and games are like from an actual gamer.

This makes your affiliate links directly relevant, and in your advertising disclosure you can let them know that by clicking your link they are helping to support your business and not AI. This will resonate strongly with the anti-AI generations and shoppers. It is also required by the FTC and some international groups that you use advertising disclosures, so you might as well.

See also: Only 28% Of Americans Trust AI Search – And That Gap Is Your SEO Opening

There is affordable technology from third parties like ThoughtMetrics (I have zero relationship with them, just a happy user) that shows all touchpoints in a customer journey (and repeat purchases for LTV). If you didn’t use your affiliate link, you won’t be in the running for credit or a commission. In another program, we reconcile at the end of the month and manually add anything that didn’t track. If that click didn’t happen, you would not be making as much money.

Link clicks are always going to be an issue, but they are also still working and a first line of defense in your ability to get credit for your referrals. So yes, affiliate links and clicks still matter; there are just additional layers of protection available with more advanced tracking techniques.

#7429. The $4 million Internet Invitational might become golf’s next big thing — or another bogey

You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all. I’m talking about the Internet Invitational, which recently wrapped up its second season by splitting a $4 million prize among the 16 members of the winning team.

The driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports. To create an event that could demonstrate the influence and appeal of the “YouTube golf” scene, Portnoy teamed up with Robby Berger and his Bob Does Sports brand.

The first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize. The event was put on as a response to the PGA’s uneven investment in golf personalities. The Creator Classic that had signaled the PGA’s interest in digital partnerships was not held at TPC Sawgrass in 2026.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Portnoy and Berger bet that they could outdo the PGA by fully embracing golf creators, and they doubled down in 2026, when they quadrupled the size of the Internet Invitational prize. “It’s all because of Dave, man,” Barstool Sports video editor Brendan Jones told Golf magazine. “Dave puts up all this money, and that changes people. That’s not good or bad — it just changes the way that people act, right? Dave’s big thing with anything that we do at Barstool, it’s like, what are the stakes? Why do people care? How are we going to get anything out of them?”

In this case, people care because the proceedings were sillier, wackier, and more relatable than anything a PGA-sanctioned event could deliver. There were breakout stars like Paige Spiranac, wildly varied handicaps, and plenty of substance use during the tournament. And the fans loved it. Viewership hit 3.5 million during the first 24 hours and ballooned past 11 million views within a week.

“When you put the average Joe, who’s not a great golfer— that, to I think a lot of people, was riveting,” Berger told The Hollywood Reporter. “I mean, it’s kind of what Bob Does Sports was built off of.”

As exciting as the action may have been, the Internet Invitational wasn’t free from drama. Nelk member Salim Sirur‘s excessive drinking and Sam Heung Min‘s criticisms related to rules enforcement added controversy to the event’s conclusion. Given Portnoy’s controversial past and the indiscretions of some big names in the YouTube golf community (looking at you, Good Good), one wonders how long the Internet Invitational can sustain its positive momentum.

But the success of the tournament’s second iteration can’t be ignored. With the decline of LIV Golf and the presence of elite golfers on YouTube, there’s an opportunity for creators to build a viable alternative to the PGA Tour. To do that will take continued dedication from the people who made the Internet Invitational happen — and the golfers might want to cut down on the drinking, too.

Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all users and uses it for the hardest AI Overview questions, two days into a core update.

Google made Gemini 4 Hydrogen the default model in AI Mode for all users worldwide, starting today. Sites that track how often AI Mode cites them now have a new model to account for.

In an X thread announcing the change, Robby Stein, VP of Product for Google Search, said Hydrogen is also “being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google’s Search post says the model is available globally in Search for all users.

The switch came two days into the November core update, which was still rolling out as of 2:05 p.m. ET today.

The Search post says Hydrogen is able to handle multi-part inquiries, inquiries that contain typos, highly specific inquiries, and follow commands more thoroughly than previous versions of Search.

The post from Search says that Hydrogen also allows for better query fan-out. Query fan-out refers to how Search simultaneously executes multiple queries across each of the subtopics of an inquiry. According to the post, the result is what Google calls “connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before,” and this includes websites which users may have never stumbled upon themselves. Stein’s thread says that the fan-out improvements result in showing more links to the web. Neither the post nor Stein’s thread provide counts for links or sites.

The post references more visual aids in answers through use of images, structured responses, comparison tables and additional customized tools available to users; additionally, the answers provided will be more nuanced in all languages supported by AI Mode.

The last default change I covered was at I/O back in May when Gemini 3.5 Flash became the global default for AI Mode for everyone. Neither the Search post nor Stein’s post said what Hydrogen replaced.

Stein’s thread has Hydrogen handling the hardest AI Overview questions but doesn’t say which questions count as hardest or what answers the rest. The Search post doesn’t mention AI Overviews.

Google made Gemini 3 the default model for AI Overviews globally in January. At the time, I noted that Google had described plans to send complex questions to Gemini 3 and simpler ones to faster models, and hadn’t said whether that would apply to AI Overviews.

Citation data you pull for AI Mode or AI Overviews this month now spans a model change on Nov. 12. The change applies to AI Mode’s default answers and to the hardest AI Overview questions.

Nov. 12 falls inside the core update window, which began Nov. 10. Logging both dates lets you compare your tracking data before and after each one, rather than reading this month as a single change.

Google’s claim that there are more links doesn’t include figures. You can check how it applies to your site by looking at the citation and referral numbers in your own reports.

Although the Search Status Dashboard shows that the November core update is rolling out, its completion date will be logged as the second date, after Nov. 12.

You should watch for an announcement from Google on which AI Overview questions are classified as hardest so you can see how much of your AI Overview tracking will reflect the change.

#7422. X offers to let creators chill–it’ll pay clippers for them, and give them a kickback too

Everyone is competing for creators’ attention lately–but X has been doing it for years.

Its latest bid: a clipping tool that pays both creators and clippers for reposting bite-sized pieces of longer content.

“Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X,” the platform said in a company post. “Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so new viewers can find your work and keep watching. Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X. The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards. Everyone wins when great moments travel.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

As you very likely know, clipping is the method du jour for creators to spread the word about their stuff. Sometimes fans clip for free/for the love of the game, but in many cases, creators pay people to clip their long-form videos and spread the shorter vids across platforms, hoping to drive more people to their full-length YouTube videos, Twitch streams, or podcast episodes.

With its clipping tool–which, from the announcement video, looks like a basic trimmer with no real editing capabilities–X is telling creators, Hey, you don’t have to worry about hiring clippers for our platform. We’ll do it. That could be an upside for creators who don’t want to compensate people themselves.

Grab your favorite moment from any video, add your take, and post it without leaving X.

Creators: every clip credits your original video and links back to it, so new viewers can find your work and keep watching.

Clippers: you now have an easy, native way to share moments from your favorite creators directly on X.

The best part? Both the original creator and the clipper can earn from views on the clip through Original Content Rewards.

Everyone wins when great moments travel. Clipping is one more step toward making X the best place to create, grow and earn.

And for clippers, the upside is financial. Clippers who aren’t directly hired/otherwise greenlit by creators generally don’t make money off their reposts, since reuploaded material can be (and usually is) copyright claimed by the original creator. A successful claim will divert any earnings to that creator. Makes sense, since it’s their content.

X, however, is offering a blanket green light. We’re not sure Elon Musk‘s platform will pay enough to tempt pro clippers, but it might appeal to aspiring clippers who seek a lower barrier to entry.

To be clear, though, we don’t know how much X will pay clippers. It says they’ll earn money through its rewards program, which pays a set amount based on engagement metrics, but how will revenue be split between creator and clipper?

Also worth noting: Not everyone can join the rewards program. X has to approve you first.

Like we mentioned above, this is far from X’s first attempt to woo creators. Not long after Musk bought it, X (still called Twitter at that point…RIP) increased its max video length to 60 minutes, clearly hoping to pull some YouTubers. Musk himself personally appealed to MrBeast, who obliged and put a long-form video on X in early 2024; he did not seem overly impressed by the results, and has stayed firmly on YouTube, where he’s the biggest fish around.

Other tweaks X has made include abolishing Twitter’s iconic character limit (thus attempting to challenge YouTube text posts as well as newsletter hubs like Substack), letting creators paywall posts, and adding a “completely redesigned livestreaming control room.” That last launch came with a promise to shell out a total of $1 million to streamers who went live on X.

#7417. Have you heard? MatPat’s return, Tubi CEO’s next move, and Trisha Paytas’ payday.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly said in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

WhatCultureGaming launches new YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The plan is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

Anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

Elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

Meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a new dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

Hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have big shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

The first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the new ceremony.

Kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a new type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game launches, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

Barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

Celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

Shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a new gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets users decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on big purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

Google Ads introduces an Invalid Traffic Overview Card showing estimated savings, post-billing credits, and campaign-level reports. Here's what advertisers need to know.

Google Ads is rolling out a new Invalid Traffic Overview Card that shows advertisers how much invalid activity its systems filter before billing, along with credits issued after billing.

Until now, advertisers had to look across campaign reports and monthly billing statements to find that information. The new card brings those figures into one view, with additional reporting available by day and campaign.

Ginny Marvin, Google Ads Liaison, announced the rollout on LinkedIn and shared more details in the latest Ads Decoded newsletter.

The global rollout began this week, and the feature is also available in Search Ads 360 for Google Ads accounts.

Advertisers can find the new card on the Google Ads Overview page, under the Campaigns tab.

Google has long used automated systems and manual reviews to filter invalid ad interactions, including bot activity, accidental clicks, and attempts to artificially inflate traffic.

Most of that activity is caught before billing, so advertisers aren’t charged for those interactions.

The new card includes three reporting areas:

Clicking “View details” opens a daily trend chart and campaign table. Advertisers can also access the monthly invoices where credits were applied.

The estimated savings figure is the main addition to this information. Advertisers could already review invalid click metrics, but those reports didn’t show the estimated dollar amount Google had prevented from being charged.

According to Marvin, Google’s systems catch the majority of invalid traffic before it reaches an advertiser’s invoice.

Google Ads locks standard campaign metrics at month-end to match billing records. If Google detects more invalid traffic after that, any credits issued won’t change the Cost or CPA figures in the main Campaigns table.

Advertisers who want to see those adjustments reflected in their performance metrics can use the Invalid Activity Credit: Search & PMax report.

Available in Report editor, it includes 10 columns, such as Adjusted cost and Adjusted cost / conv. Credits are attributed to the dates the ads originally ran, even when Google issued them later.

This gives advertisers a way to review Search and Performance Max costs with post-billing invalid activity credits factored in, without relying solely on the standard Campaigns table.

The campaign-level breakdowns should make it easier to see where Google is filtering invalid activity, although the estimated savings figures will need some context.

A campaign with significantly more spend could show higher estimated savings simply because it’s generating more traffic. Comparing those dollar amounts alone won’t necessarily tell advertisers which campaigns have greater traffic quality concerns.

There’s also a limit to what the numbers can tell us. The card reflects activity Google’s systems have identified as invalid, but it doesn’t establish how much fraudulent traffic may have gone undetected.

For lead generation accounts, invalid traffic reporting won’t necessarily explain why fake or low-quality leads are continuing to come in.

Marvin addressed this in the Ads Decoded newsletter: Google’s systems can filter invalid ad interactions, but bad leads can still come from legitimate clicks or submissions that never originated from an ad.

An account could have relatively little invalid traffic reported in Google Ads and still struggle with lead quality. Advertisers dealing with those issues will need to compare the reporting against their CRM data rather than assuming Google’s invalid traffic figures tell the whole story.

Featured image: Primakov (screenshot from Google Ads Decoded Newsletter) / Shutterstock
